title: Fort Hood shooter: Pentagon plans public livestream of firing squad execution | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

The Pentagon said Thursday it will livestream the military’s first firing squad execution in decades, allowing the public to watch as the man who killed 13 people in a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood is put to death.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth vowed in an interview this week to let the public watch a firing squad execute Nidal Hasan at the same base in Texas where he carried out the massacre.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth told far-right podcaster Jack Posobiec in an interview aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln on Wednesday, drawing swift backlash from both sides of the aisle.

A Pentagon official said Thursday that the execution — which Hegseth recommended and President Donald Trump approved — “will be livestreamed” and Hegseth confirmed it in a post on X.

Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle set the date for Hasan’s execution for December 3 at 1 p.m. local time.

Hegseth said, “We’re going to do it at one o’clock, which is when he did it, and it’s going to be soldiers with rifles executing the firing squad.”

Earlier on Thursday, the Pentagon had referred questions about how the execution would be publicized to the Army, who did not respond to CNN.

Hasan was convicted in July 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted murder. During his trial, he told the panel of 13 officers that he was targeting soldiers who would deploy to Afghanistan and “were going to engage in an illegal war.” On the day of the shooting, he started at the medical processing center at Fort Hood, firing on troops there to collectmedical checks before they deployed. He then followed soldiers out the back door of the processing center as they fled and was confronted by police, with whom Hasan exchanged gunfire and was eventually struck.

The execution by firing squad would be the first of its kind carried out by the US Army since World War II. Hegseth said in the interview that he liked “the mentality we had in World War II, which was win. Which was understand when the enemy attacks you, you stand your ground.”

Hegseth’s pledge to let the public watch the firing squad execution has drawn condemnation on both sides of the aisle.

Republican Sen. Thom Tillis late Thursday called it “beyond disgusting.” Hesaid on X,“Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.”

Sen. Chris Murphy, a Democrat, is stunned — telling CNN’s Erin Burnett that public executions are “medieval.”

“I mean, that’s disgusting, what is he mimicking ISIS executions?” Murphy said. “That’s what America has become? That’s pretty extraordinary.”

The president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops denounced the plan on Friday calling it a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death.”

“It is with shock and great sorrow that I have learned of the Department of War’s decision to publicly livestream the execution of Nidal Hassan. Our God is the God of life. In no way can Hassan’s actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered,” Archbishop Paul Coakley saidin a statementreleased Friday.

A public livestream of Hasan’s execution could potentially violate the Army regulations governing military capital punishment. Army Regulation 190-55 specifies the types of people permitted to witness a military execution, and it also bars minors from watching the punishment. But the Army’s provost marshal general — a general who oversees military law enforcement — is permitted to waive provisions of the regulation so long as the waiver doesn’t violate the law or a higher binding regulation.

This story has been updated with additional details.
